summary: BIER is a new architecture for forwarding multicast packets. A packet is marked at the ingress router with the set of destinations, and routers forward it without building multicast trees or keeping per-flow state. This document describes the architecture.

eli5.summary: Instead of the post office tracking every mailing list, each envelope lists all its recipients, and each stop just reads the list and forwards copies.

does bier need per flow state
subtitle: Multicast where each packet carries a bit for every destination router, so the core keeps no per-flow state.

tldr.problem: Conventional multicast builds distribution trees and makes routers in the middle keep state for each flow.
tldr.mechanism: The ingress router adds a BIER header whose BitString has one bit per egress router. Each router uses a forwarding table to split the packet by next hop, keeping only the bits reachable that way in each copy.
tldr.outcome: Packets follow unicast paths to each egress router with no tree-building protocol and no duplicate delivery. The cost is a limited BitString length and a dependence on a routing underlay and an overlay defined elsewhere.

today: RFC 8279 was published in November 2017, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The encapsulations, IGP and BGP advertisement extensions and overlay procedures it defers to are specified in companion documents.

sections.title: The BIER Idea
sections.content:
RFC 8279 specifies a new architecture for forwarding multicast packets, called Bit Index Explicit Replication (BIER). It gives optimal forwarding through a multicast domain without a protocol for building multicast distribution trees and without per-flow state in intermediate nodes.

A BIER-capable router is a Bit-Forwarding Router (BFR). A packet enters the BIER domain at a Bit-Forwarding Ingress Router (BFIR) and leaves at one or more Bit-Forwarding Egress Routers (BFERs). A router in between is a transit BFR, and one router can play all roles for different traffic.

The BFIR wraps the packet in a BIER header containing a BitString, where each bit stands for one BFR-id. Setting a bit means that BFER should receive the packet. Because the set of receivers is written into the header, the packet is not sent to any BFER that does not need it.

The RFC contrasts this with an earlier proposal that listed egress nodes as IP addresses: one IPv6 address takes as many bits as 128 BFER bits.
sections.eli5: Instead of the post office remembering every mailing list, each envelope has a checklist of who should get a copy.

sections.title: BFR-ids, BFR-prefixes and BitStrings
sections.content:
Each BFR gets a BFR-prefix per sub-domain: an IPv4 or IPv6 address of the BFR, ideally a loopback address, which must be routable in that sub-domain. A BFR-id is a number in the range 1 to 65535 that uniquely identifies a BFIR or BFER in a sub-domain. The value 0 is not a legal BFR-id. A BIER domain has at least one sub-domain, the default sub-domain 0, and sub-domain ids range from 0 to 255.

To place a BFR-id N in a packet, the encoding uses a Set Identifier (SI) and a bit position. SI is the integer part of (N-1)/BitStringLength, and the bit is ((N-1) modulo BitStringLength)+1. With a BitStringLength of 256, BFR-ids 13, 126 and 235 share SI 0, while BFR-id 257 needs SI 1 and so a second copy of the packet.

It is RECOMMENDED to assign BFR-ids densely, starting from 1, so fewer SIs and copies are needed. A BFR MUST support SI values 0 to 15 and MAY support 0 to 255. The total number of BFR-ids is the BitStringLength times the number of SIs, so 64 bits and 256 SIs give only 16384 BFR-ids.

BFRs advertise their BFR-prefix, BFR-id and Disposition BitStringLengths, for example through OSPF or IS-IS extensions defined in companion documents. If two BFRs advertise the same BFR-id in a sub-domain, a BFR must log an error and a BFIR must not use that BFR-id in packets.
sections.eli5: Every house gets a number. The checklist is a row of tiny boxes, and ticking box 13 means house 13 gets a copy. When there are more houses than boxes, a second checklist is used.

sections.title: Three Layers
sections.content:
The architecture has three layers.

  • The routing underlay sets up adjacencies between BFRs and picks the best paths. Typically it is the IGP's default topology, such as OSPF. By default each sub-domain uses the default topology of the unicast IGP, and each sub-domain MUST be tied to a single underlay.
  • The BIER layer advertises BFR information, imposes and removes the BIER header, and forwards and modifies packets in transit.
  • The multicast flow overlay tells a BFIR which BFERs need a given flow, and tells a BFER how to forward a packet it receives. The RFC gives Multicast VPN (RFC 6513 and RFC 6514) as one example, and says an SDN controller could also be used.

The protocols of the underlay and the overlay are outside the scope of this document.
sections.eli5: The roads are the underlay, the checklist-and-copying rules are the BIER layer, and the list of who wants which show is the overlay.

sections.title: How a BFR Forwards a Packet
sections.content:
A BFR builds a Bit Index Routing Table (BIRT) mapping each BFR-id to the destination's BFR-prefix and the next-hop neighbor (BFR-NBR). From it, the Bit Index Forwarding Table (BIFT) is derived. Rows with the same SI and BFR-NBR are combined by OR into a Forwarding Bit Mask (F-BM).

For a packet, the BFR repeats these steps. If the BitString is all zeroes, discard the packet. Find the least significant set bit k. If it identifies the BFR itself, send a copy to the multicast flow overlay and clear that bit. Otherwise look up entry k in the BIFT, copy the packet, AND the copy's BitString with the F-BM and send it to the BFR-NBR, then AND the original's BitString with the inverse of the F-BM. Repeat.

The number of table lookups equals the number of neighbors the packet goes to, not the number of destinations. A null next hop covers unused or unreachable BFR-ids, and those packets are discarded. If the header has a TTL it is decremented, and an entropy field SHOULD be respected for load balancing.

A BFER passes the payload to the overlay after removing the BIER header. A BIER packet cannot pass directly between BIER domains; it must be decapsulated at the boundary.
sections.eli5: At each crossroads you look at who is still on the checklist, send a copy down each road with only the houses on that road, and cross those houses off what you keep.

sections.title: A Worked Example
sections.content:
The RFC's topology has BFR-A connected to BFR-B, which connects to BFR-C and BFR-E, with BFR-C connecting to BFR-D and BFR-F. It uses a BitStringLength of 4 only for illustration. BFR-D has BFR-id 1, BFR-F has 2, BFR-E has 3 and BFR-A has 4.

In the second example the BFIR, BFR-A, must reach BFER-D and BFER-E, so the BitString is 0101. BFR-A's BIFT entry 1 has F-BM 0111 and next hop B, so it sends one copy to B and its own BitString becomes 0000. At B, entry 1 sends a copy with 0001 to C, and the remaining 0100 goes to E through entry 3. C forwards on to D.

The packet is replicated only where paths diverge, and each BFER gets exactly one copy.
sections.eli5: The first town sends one pile of mail to the next town. There the pile is split in two, one pile for each road, and each pile only lists the houses on its road.

sections.title: ECMP, Loops and Non-BIER Nodes
sections.content:
For equal-cost multipath (ECMP), two procedures are defined. In non-deterministic ECMP, a BIFT entry can list more than one BFR-NBR, each with its own F-BM, and the BFR must use the F-BM of the neighbor it picks. This minimizes copies but the path to a BFER can depend on which other BFERs are in the packet, so a flow can switch paths. In deterministic ECMP, several BIFTs are used, each with one path per destination, and a hash of the entropy field picks the BIFT. The two procedures interoperate.

Loops and duplicates: copies never share a BFER and a BFER clears its own bit before forwarding, so duplicate delivery is impossible. Loops occur only if the underlay has a loop, and even then no duplicates are delivered. This removes the need for a Reverse Path Forwarding check.

Non-BIER nodes: if an adjacent node does not support BIER, a BFR can remove it from its copy of the IGP shortest-path tree and re-parent its children, sending packets through a unicast tunnel such as MPLS. The tunnel's TTL should not be copied into the BIER header.

Mixed BitStringLengths: a BitStringLength Compatibility Check detects mismatches. A BFR facing one can discard the packet, re-encapsulate it, or treat the neighbor as non-BIER. To migrate from length X to Y, first make all BFRs accept both, then switch the BFIRs, then optionally drop X.
sections.eli5: If two roads lead to the same place, you may pick either, but you should stick to your pick. If a town has no BIER mail carrier, you send the mail past it in a sealed bag.

sections.title: Operations and Security
sections.content:
The operational section describes BIER as a simplification of IP multicast: no tree-building control plane, no per-flow forwarding state, no RPF and no Rendezvous Point. Per-flow monitoring of (S,G) entries is not provided in a BIER node. The text says BIER can converge right after the unicast table, regardless of the number of flows. Each BFER needs a unique BFR-id configured and advertised in the IGP.

On security, BIER inherits the considerations of the chosen overlay and underlay. A modified BitString can misdeliver packets, and setting every bit can cause denial of service, as can a compromised BFIR. Every BFR MUST know which interfaces lead into the BIER domain, and BIER packets MUST NOT be accepted from outside it. Insecure advertisement procedures could cause incorrect delivery. This RFC has an IANA Considerations section.
sections.eli5: Only trusted mail trucks may enter the mail system. Otherwise, a prankster could tick every box and flood every house.
